p.src: After reading the poems, everyone praised their ingenuity and subtlety. Baochai spoke first. “The first eight poems are all supported by the historical records, but the last two cannot be substantiated, and we do not understand them very well either. It would be better to compose two others.” Daiyu hastily stopped her. “Sister Bao, you are far too hidebound and affected about this. Though these two poems have no basis in the histories, and though we have never read such unofficial tales and do not know the details, surely you cannot say that we have never seen a couple of plays? Even a three-year-old knows these stories, let alone us!” “That is exactly right,” said Tanchun. Li Wan added, “Besides, she actually visited these places herself. These two stories may be unsubstantiated, but throughout the ages errors have been repeated as truth, and meddlesome people have even deliberately fabricated historic sites to deceive others. For instance, when we went up to the capital that year, we saw three or four places claiming to be Lord Guan's grave alone. The deeds of Lord Guan's life are all well attested, so how could he have so many graves? People of later generations naturally revered him for the man he had been, and some of those tales may well have been contrived out of that reverence. When I later consulted the Guangyu Ji, I found that it was not only Lord Guan who had numerous graves: since ancient times, celebrated people have often had no shortage of tombs, and unsubstantiated historic sites are more numerous still. These two poems may lack historical proof, but the stories appear in storytellers' tales and stage plays, and even in the annotations on fortune sticks. Old and young, men and women—all know them and repeat them in everyday speech. Besides, it is not as though she had been reading the librettos of The Western Chamber or The Peony Pavilion and might be corrupted by improper books. There is really no harm in it. Let them remain.” Only after hearing this did Baochai let the matter drop. They all tried guessing the answers for a while, but none of their guesses was right.

p.src: Winter days were short, and before they knew it, it was again time for supper in the front rooms, so they all went over to dine. Someone came and reported to Lady Wang, “Xiren's elder brother, Hua Zifang, has come to say that their mother is gravely ill and longs to see her daughter. He has come to beg your ladyship's leave to take Xiren home for a visit.” Lady Wang replied, “They are mother and daughter; how could we refuse to let her go?” She immediately summoned Xifeng, explained the matter to her, and told her to make whatever arrangements she thought appropriate.

Someone came and reported to Lady Wang, “Xiren's elder brother, Hua Zifang, has come to say that their mother is gravely ill and longs to see her daughter.
He has come to beg your ladyship's leave to take Xiren home for a visit.”
Lady Wang replied, “They are mother and daughter; how could we refuse to let her go?”
She immediately summoned Xifeng, explained the matter to her, and told her to make whatever arrangements she thought appropriate.

p.src: Xifeng assented and returned to her room, where she instructed Zhou Rui's wife to tell Xiren what had happened. She further instructed her, “Summon one of the married women who accompany us when we go out. The two of you, together with two young maids, are to escort Xiren. Have four older, dependable men assigned outside to attend the carriages. Order a large carriage for you women to ride in and a smaller one for the maids.” Zhou Rui's wife assented and was just about to leave when Xifeng added, “Xiren is a sensible girl, but tell her this from me: she is to put on several brightly colored garments, pack a large bundle of clothes to take with her, and see that both the bundle and the hand warmer are good ones. Before she leaves, have her come here so that I may look her over.” Zhou Rui's wife assented and went off.

p.src: After some time, Xiren duly appeared dressed for the journey, while two maids and Zhou Rui's wife carried her hand warmer and bundle of clothes. Xifeng saw that Xiren's hair was adorned with several gold hairpins and pearl ornaments and looked quite splendid. She was wearing a peach-red silver-squirrel jacket woven in the hundred-children pattern, a scallion-green padded skirt embroidered in colored silks and couched gold, and over these a blue-satin jacket lined with gray squirrel. Xifeng smiled. “All three of these garments were gifts to you from Her Ladyship, and very fine they are. But this outer jacket is a little too plain, and it will be cold wearing it now. You ought to wear one lined with long fur.” Xiren smiled. “Her Ladyship has given me only this gray-squirrel one and another lined with silver squirrel. She said she would give me a long-fur one toward the New Year, but I have not received it yet.” Xifeng smiled. “I have a long-fur one myself. I dislike the way its russet-gold fur lies and was just going to have it altered. Never mind—take it and wear it for now. When Her Ladyship has one made for you at New Year, I shall have mine altered then; we will simply count it as your repaying me in kind.” Everyone laughed. “Your Ladyship is always saying things like that. Year after year you spend so freely and make good out of your own pocket no one knows how many things for Her Ladyship. Truly, you have laid out more than can be counted, yet when have you ever settled accounts with her? Yet now you deliberately make this petty little remark just to amuse us.” Xifeng laughed. “How could Her Ladyship be expected to think of such details? After all, these are not official household expenses; yet if they are neglected, they reflect poorly on us all. There is nothing for it but to bear some loss myself and see that everyone is respectably dressed. If it earns me a good name, I suppose that will suffice. If each of them went about looking like a scorched scroll, people would laugh at me first and say that, for all my management, I had turned the servants into beggars.” Hearing this, they all exclaimed admiringly, “Who could be as wise and discerning as Your Ladyship! You are considerate of Her Ladyship above you and tenderly look after the servants below.” As they spoke, Xifeng ordered Ping'er to bring out the dark-blue tapestry jacket with eight roundels and a celestial-horse-fur lining that she had worn the day before, and gave it to Xiren. She then inspected the bundle and found only a lined wrapper of patterned damask with a pale-red silk lining, containing no more than two partly worn padded jackets and a fur outer jacket. Xifeng therefore ordered Ping'er to bring out a bundle wrapper of broadcloth lined with jade-colored silk and told her to pack a snow cloak as well.

p.src: Ping'er went and brought them out: one was a slightly worn cloak of scarlet Russian felt, the other of scarlet feather gauze. Xiren said, “Even one is more than I deserve.” Ping'er laughed. “You take the felt one. I brought this other one out while I was about it so that someone could take it to Miss Xing. In yesterday's heavy snow everyone else had one—either Russian felt, feather satin, or feather gauze—and those dozen or so scarlet cloaks looked splendidly uniform against the snow. She alone wore that old felt cape, which made her hunched shoulders and shrunken figure look all the more pitiful. Let us give her this one now.” Xifeng laughed. “She takes my things and gives them away without so much as asking me. As if I did not squander enough myself, having you egg me on makes it better still!” The others laughed. “It is only because you have always been dutiful to Her Ladyship and kind to those beneath you. If you were habitually stingy, cared only for possessions, and gave no thought to your servants, how would Miss Ping'er ever dare do such a thing?” Xifeng laughed. “That is why, of all people, she understands perhaps three-tenths of what is in my heart.” Then she cautioned Xiren, “If your mother recovers, all is well; but if she is beyond help, stay there, send someone to tell me, and I shall have your bedding sent separately. Do not use their bedding or their hairdressing things.” She also instructed Zhou Rui's wife, “You naturally know the rules here, so there is no need for me to remind you.” Zhou Rui's wife replied, “We know them all. When we arrive, we shall have all their people withdraw. If she stays, we shall certainly require one or two separate inner rooms.” With that, she followed Xiren out and ordered lanterns prepared; they then rode by carriage to Hua Zifang's home, and we shall say no more of their journey.

p.src: Meanwhile, Xifeng summoned two of the matrons from Happy Red Court and instructed them, “Xiren may not return tonight. You know the senior maids well; choose two sensible ones to keep watch in Baoyu's room. Take good care of things yourselves, too, and do not let Baoyu carry on as he pleases.” The two matrons left and presently returned to report, “We have assigned Qingwen and Sheyue to his room. The four of us already take turns supervising the night watch.” Xifeng nodded when she heard this. “Urge him to bed early at night and make him rise early in the morning.” The old matrons assented and returned to the Garden. Before long, Zhou Rui's wife indeed brought word back to Xifeng: “Xiren's mother has already been laid out on her deathbed, so Xiren cannot return.” Xifeng reported the matter to Lady Wang and at once sent someone to Prospect Garden to fetch Xiren's bedding and toilet case.

p.src: Baoyu watched Qingwen and Sheyue finish arranging everything and send the things off; afterward, both maids removed the remnants of their makeup and changed their skirts and jackets. Qingwen merely sat huddled on the heated kang-cage. Sheyue laughed. “Do stop playing the young lady today. I advise you to stir yourself a little.” Qingwen replied, “There will be time enough to take your advice after all of you are gone. As long as you are here, I mean to enjoy myself.” Sheyue laughed. “Dear sister, while I make the bed, lower the cover over the full-length mirror and fasten the catch at the top. You are a little taller than I am.” As she spoke, she went to make Baoyu's bed. Qingwen sighed and laughed. “I have only just got this seat warm, and now you come bothering me.” Baoyu was sitting there troubled, wondering whether Xiren's mother was alive or dead. Hearing Qingwen's complaint, he rose and went out himself, lowered the mirror cover, fastened its catch, then returned laughing. “You two keep warm. It is all done.” Qingwen laughed. “It seems I am not destined to keep warm after all. I have just remembered that the bed-warmer has not been brought in.” Sheyue said, “Trust you to remember that! He never uses a bed-warmer, and our heated cage is warm, unlike the cold kang in that room. We can do without it today.” Baoyu laughed. “But if both of you sleep up there and no one stays out here with me, I shall be terribly frightened and unable to sleep all night.” Qingwen said, “I shall stay here. Sheyue can sleep outside his bedchamber.” While they were speaking, the second watch arrived. Sheyue had already lowered the curtains, moved the lamp, and lit incense; after helping Baoyu into bed, the two maids finally went to sleep.

p.src: Qingwen remained on the heated cage, while Sheyue slept just outside the warm chamber. After the third watch, Baoyu called for Xiren in his sleep. He called twice, but no one answered. Waking, he remembered that Xiren was away and could not help laughing at himself. Qingwen was already awake. Laughing, she called to Sheyue, “Even I have woken, yet she, lying right beside him, knows nothing. She sleeps like a corpse!” Sheyue turned over, yawned, and laughed. “He called Xiren. What has that to do with me?” Then she asked what he wanted. Baoyu wanted some tea, so Sheyue hurriedly rose wearing only a little padded jacket of red silk. Baoyu said, “Put on my jacket before you go, or you may catch cold.” Hearing this, Sheyue reached back and threw over herself Baoyu's full-fronted warm jacket with a marten-fur collar, which he used when rising at night. She stepped down and washed her hands in the basin, poured out a cup of warm water, and brought the large rinsing bowl. After Baoyu had rinsed his mouth, she took a teacup from the tea cabinet, rinsed it first with warm water, poured half a bowl of tea from the warm pot, and handed it to Baoyu to drink; then she too rinsed her mouth and drank half a bowl. Qingwen laughed. “Dear sister, spare a sip for me too.” Sheyue laughed. “You are growing more impudent by the minute!” Qingwen said, “Dear sister, tomorrow night you need not lift a finger. I shall wait on you all night. How about that?” At this, Sheyue had no choice but to help her rinse her mouth too, then pour half a bowl of tea and give it to her to drink. Sheyue laughed. “You two stay awake and talk. I am going out for a little walk and shall be back soon.” Qingwen laughed. “There is a ghost outside waiting for you.” Baoyu said, “There must be a bright moon outside. We shall talk, so go along if you like.” Even as he spoke, he coughed twice.

Baoyu said, “There must be a bright moon outside. We shall talk, so go along if you like.”
Even as he spoke, he coughed twice.

p.src: Sheyue opened the back door and lifted the felt curtain to look outside; the moonlight was indeed beautiful. Qingwen waited until she had gone out, intending to give her a fright for fun. Being hardier than the others and unafraid of the cold, she put on no outer garment, but climbed quietly down from the heated couch in only her short jacket and crept out after her. Baoyu laughingly warned her, “Mind you don't catch cold. This is no game.” Qingwen merely waved her hand and went out through the door. The moonlight was like water. Suddenly a light breeze sprang up, piercing her skin and penetrating to the bone, and she could not help shuddering all over. She thought to herself, “No wonder people say you mustn't let the wind strike you when your body is warm. This chill really is severe.” Just as she was about to frighten Sheyue, she heard Baoyu call loudly from inside, “Qingwen has gone out!” Qingwen hurriedly turned back inside and said with a laugh, “As if I could frighten her to death! Why must you always fuss like some timid old woman?” Baoyu laughed. “It isn't that I fear she'll be harmed by the fright. First, it would be bad if you caught cold; second, taken unawares, she would surely cry out. If she woke the others, instead of saying we were only playing, they would say that no sooner had Xiren been away for one night than you all began seeing ghosts and spirits. Come and tuck in this side of my quilt.” At this Qingwen came over and tucked it in. When she slipped a hand beneath the quilt to warm it, Baoyu laughed and said, “What an icy hand! I told you that you would get chilled.” He saw that Qingwen's cheeks were as red as rouge, but when he touched them, they too felt icy cold. Baoyu said, “Quick, get under the quilt and warm yourself.” Before he had finished speaking, the door opened with a click and Sheyue hurried in, laughing. “What a fright I had! In the darkness behind the rockery, I saw what looked like a person crouching there. I was just about to scream when I realized it was that big golden pheasant. It took flight at the sight of me and flew into the light, and only then did I see it clearly. If I had rashly shouted, I would have roused the whole household.” As she spoke, she washed her hands, then laughed and asked, “How did I fail to see Qingwen when she went out? She must have gone out to frighten me.” Baoyu laughed. “Here she is, warming herself! If I hadn't called out so quickly, you really would have had another fright.” Qingwen laughed. “There was no need for me to frighten the little minx; she had already scared herself silly.” As she spoke, she went back to her own bed and slipped under the quilt. Sheyue said, “You mean you went out dressed so trimly and lightly, like an acrobat riding a bareback horse?” Baoyu laughed. “That is exactly how she went.” Sheyue said, “You little wretch, you certainly chose a fine time for it! Stand outside a little longer and see if the cold doesn't split your skin.”

p.src: Having first been chilled and now grown warm again, Qingwen involuntarily sneezed twice. Baoyu sighed. “There now! You have caught cold after all.” Sheyue laughed. “She was already complaining of feeling unwell this morning and has eaten nothing all day. Yet instead of taking care of herself, she still insists on playing tricks on people. If she falls ill tomorrow, she will have only herself to blame.” Baoyu asked, “Does your forehead feel hot?” Qingwen coughed twice and replied, “It is nothing. Since when have I been so delicate?” As she spoke, the chiming clock on the curio shelf in the outer room struck twice. An old nurse keeping watch outside coughed twice and said, “Young ladies, go to sleep. You can talk again tomorrow.” Only then did Baoyu say with a quiet laugh, “Let us stop talking, or we shall set them talking again.” After that, they all settled down to sleep. When she rose the next morning, Qingwen found that her nose was indeed somewhat blocked, her voice was thick, and she had no desire to move. Baoyu said, “Quick, don't let anyone know! If Her Ladyship hears of it, she will make you move home to recuperate again. Home may be pleasant enough, but it is colder there and not as good as staying here. Lie down in the inner room. I shall have a doctor summoned and bring him quietly through the back door to examine you.” Qingwen said, “Even so, you had better inform the Young Mistress. Otherwise, when the doctor comes and someone asks about it, what shall we say?” Baoyu saw the sense in this and summoned an old nurse, instructing her, “Go and tell the Young Mistress that Qingwen merely caught a slight chill and that it is nothing serious. Xiren is away too, and if Qingwen goes home to recover, there will be even fewer people here. Have a doctor summoned and bring him quietly through the back door to examine her, but do not report it to Her Ladyship.” The old nurse was gone for some time, then returned with this reply: “The Young Mistress knows. She says that if two doses of medicine cure her, well and good; but if she does not improve, it would still be best for her to leave. Illness is rife just now. Infecting others would be a small matter beside the importance of safeguarding the young ladies' health.” Qingwen lay in the warm chamber, coughing incessantly. When she heard this, she cried out angrily, “Do they think I have the plague, that they are afraid I shall infect someone? Once I have left this place, let us see that none of you ever suffers so much as a headache or fever for the rest of your lives!” With that, she really made as if to rise. Baoyu hurriedly held her down and said with a smile, “Don't be angry. It is her responsibility, after all. She merely said it for fear that Her Ladyship might hear of this and blame her. You are always quick-tempered, so naturally your liver-fire is flaring up now.”

p.src: While they were still talking, someone announced that the doctor had arrived. Baoyu came over and concealed himself behind a bookcase. He saw two or three elderly matrons from the rear gate escorting a doctor inside. All the maids there withdrew, and three or four elderly matrons lowered the great scarlet embroidered curtain before the warm chamber; from behind it Qingwen extended one hand and nothing more. When the doctor saw that two of the fingernails on this hand were fully three inches long and still bore bright-red traces of balsam dye, he hurriedly turned his head away. One of the elderly matrons promptly covered the hand with a handkerchief. Only then did the doctor feel her pulse for a while. Rising, he went into the outer room and told the matrons, “The young lady's illness is due to an external infection combined with internal stagnation. The prevailing weather has been unhealthy of late, so it may be considered a mild case of cold-induced fever. Fortunately, the young lady ordinarily eats little, and the wind-cold is not severe. Her blood and vital energy are naturally somewhat weak, and she has merely happened to catch a touch of it. Two doses of medicine to disperse the infection should make her well.” Having said this, he followed the matrons out again.

p.src: By then Li Wan had sent word to the people at the rear gate and to the maids throughout the garden that they were to keep out of sight, so the doctor saw only the garden scenery and not a single woman. Presently, after leaving the garden gate, he sat down in the duty room of the pages who guarded it and wrote out a prescription. An elderly matron said, “Please do not leave just yet, doctor. Our young master is particular and may still have something to say.” The doctor hastily asked, “Was that not a young lady just now, but a young gentleman? That room looked exactly like a young lady's boudoir, and a curtain was lowered as well. How could the patient have been a gentleman?” The elderly matron laughed quietly. “Good doctor, no wonder the pages said just now that a new doctor had been summoned today. You truly know nothing of our household. That room belongs to our young master, and the patient was a maid in his service—an older maid, to be sure, but no young lady of the family. If it had been a young lady's boudoir and the young lady herself were ill, do you suppose you could have entered so easily?” With that, she took the prescription inside.

p.src: When Baoyu examined it, he found perilla, platycodon, siler, schizonepeta, and other herbs listed at the top, followed farther down by immature bitter orange and ephedra. “Damn him! Damn him!” cried Baoyu. “How can he treat girls in exactly the same way as he treats us? Whatever internal stagnation she may have, how could she withstand bitter orange and ephedra? Who summoned this man? Send him away at once! Summon another doctor whom we know.” The old woman said, “We do not understand the principles of medicine, so we cannot tell whether a prescription is good or bad. It would be easy enough to send a page now to summon Imperial Physician Wang, but this doctor was engaged without going through the steward's office, so we must pay his sedan-and-horse fee.” “How much should he be given?” asked Baoyu. The woman replied, “Too little would look shabby. A tael of silver at least is the proper courtesy for a household of our standing.” Baoyu asked, “How much do we give Imperial Physician Wang when he comes?” The woman laughed. “Whenever Imperial Physician Wang or Imperial Physician Zhang comes, we do not pay them anything on the spot. We merely send substantial gifts at each of the four seasonal festivals every year; that is a fixed annual custom. But since this man is new and has come only this once, we must give him a tael of silver before he leaves.” On hearing this, Baoyu ordered Sheyue to fetch the silver. Sheyue said, “I have no idea where Mistress Hua keeps it.” Baoyu replied, “I often see her taking money from the small mother-of-pearl cabinet. I will go and look with you.” So the two went to the room where Baoyu stored his things and opened the mother-of-pearl cabinet. The upper compartment was filled with writing brushes, ink, fans, incense cakes, purses of every kind, handkerchiefs, and similar objects; in the lower one were several strings of cash. They then opened a drawer and at last found several pieces of silver in a small winnowing basket, together with a small steelyard for weighing silver. Sheyue picked up a piece of silver, lifted the steelyard, and asked Baoyu, “Which mark is for one tael?” Baoyu laughed. “You are asking me? How amusing! Anyone would think you had only just arrived here.” Sheyue laughed too and was about to go and ask someone else. Baoyu said, “Just choose one of the larger pieces and give it to him. We are not conducting a business transaction, so why bother calculating all this?” At this, Sheyue put down the steelyard, selected a piece, weighed it in her hand, and said with a laugh, “I expect this one is about a tael. Better to give too much than too little. We must not let that poor fellow laugh at us—not merely saying that we cannot use a steelyard, but supposing that we are deliberately being stingy.” Standing outside on the stone step, the old woman laughed and said, “That was a five-tael ingot cut in half, and this piece still weighs at least two taels! We have no shears handy just now. Put that piece back, miss, and choose a smaller one.” But Sheyue had already closed the cabinet and come out. Laughing, she said, “Who is going to search all over again? If it is a little too much, take it and be done with it.”

The woman took the silver and went off to make the arrangements.

p.src: Before long, Mingyan did indeed return with Imperial Physician Wang. After feeling the patient's pulse, he described her illness in much the same terms as the first doctor; but his prescription contained neither bitter orange nor ephedra, and included instead Chinese angelica, dried tangerine peel, white peony root, and other herbs, all in somewhat smaller doses than before. Baoyu said delightedly, “Now this is medicine suited to girls. Even when dispersing an infection, one must not go too far. When I was ill last year, I had a cold-induced fever with food stagnating inside me, yet after examining me, he still said that even I could not withstand such fierce medicines as ephedra, gypsum, and bitter orange. Compared with you, I am like an old poplar that has stood for decades in a wilderness of graves, while you are like the white crab-apple that Yun brought me in autumn, with its first blossoms newly opened. If even I cannot endure such medicine, how could you possibly bear it?” Sheyue and the others laughed. “Are there only poplars in a wilderness of graves? Are there no pines or cypresses? Of all trees, I dislike poplars most. They are such great clumsy things, with leaves no bigger than specks, and even when there is not a breath of wind, they rustle away in disorder. Of all things, you choose to compare yourself to that—it is far too vulgar.” Baoyu laughed. “I would not presume to compare myself to pines and cypresses. Even Confucius said, ‘Only when the year grows cold do we know that the pine and cypress are the last to fade.’ That shows how noble and refined those two trees are; only someone utterly shameless would compare himself to them carelessly.”

p.src: As they were speaking, the old woman returned with the medicine. Baoyu ordered them to find the little silver pot used for decocting medicine and told them to brew it over the brazier. Qingwen objected, “It ought to be sent to the tea room to be decocted. How can we fill this room with the smell of medicine?” Baoyu replied, “The fragrance of medicine is more refined than that of any flower or fruit. Immortals gather and prepare herbs, and lofty recluses gather and compound them too; medicine is the most exquisite thing there is. I was just thinking that this room had everything except the fragrance of medicine. Now at last it is complete.” Even as he spoke, he had someone set it to simmer. He also instructed Sheyue to prepare some things and send an old nurse to visit Xiren and urge her not to grieve so much. Only after everything had been properly arranged did he go to the front apartments to pay his respects to Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang and have his meal.

p.src: Just then Xifeng was discussing matters with Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang. “The days are short and the weather cold. From now on, why not have our elder sister-in-law take the young ladies’ meals with them in the Garden? When the days grow longer and warmer, it will do no harm for them to come and go again.” Lady Wang smiled. “That is a good idea too. It would be especially convenient when the wind blows or snow falls. It is no good for them to be chilled after eating; nor is it good for them to come on an empty stomach, fill their bellies with cold wind, and then press food down on top of it. It would be better to use the five large rooms just inside the rear gate of the Garden. Women are stationed there at night in any case, so we could assign two female cooks to prepare meals there solely for the sisters. They already have an allowance of fresh vegetables, which can be drawn from the steward’s office. Whether they need money or provisions, we can simply give them a share of the pheasants, roebuck, gourds, and other kinds of game.” Grandmother Jia said, “I was thinking the same thing. I was only afraid that adding another kitchen would create more trouble.” Xifeng replied, “It will not cause any extra trouble. The allowances will remain the same: whatever is added here will be deducted there. Even if it does mean a little more work, how can these young girls endure the bitter northern wind? The others may manage, but Cousin Lin least of all. Even Brother Bao cannot bear it, much less all the young ladies.” Grandmother Jia said, “That is exactly right. I meant to suggest this before, but I saw that you already had too many important matters to attend to, and now these new tasks have arisen as well...” To learn how matters turned out, read the next chapter.

Even if it does mean a little more work, how can these young girls endure the bitter northern wind? The others may manage, but Cousin Lin least of all.
Even Brother Bao cannot bear it, much less all the young ladies.”
Grandmother Jia said, “That is exactly right.

I meant to suggest this before, but I saw that you already had too many important matters to attend to, and now these new tasks have arisen as well...” To learn how matters turned out, read the next chapter.
